chapter.title: Tanning or Dyeing Extracts; Tannins and Their Derivatives; Dyes, Pigments and Other Coloring Matter; Paints and Varnishes; Putty and Other Mastics; Inks

page.h1: HTS Chapter 32: Tanning or Dyeing Extracts; Tannins and Their Derivatives; Dyes, Pigments and Other Coloring Matter; Paints and Varnishes; Putty and Other Mastics; Inks — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Exporting Paint, Pigments & Ink from the U.S.: Schedule B, TSCA, Hazmat | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Schedule B codes for paint (3208, 3209), TiO2 (3206.11), caulk (3214) and ink (3215), TSCA 12(b) export notices, UN1263 hazmat rules and export licences.
keywords: is paint considered hazardous material for shipping

intro: A U.S. exporter of paints, pigments, dyes, caulks or inks takes the same five steps as every exporter, then a short list of agency rules. **EPA** requires a TSCA section 12(b) export notice when a product contains a chemical subject to certain TSCA actions, and **DOT (PHMSA)** rules govern shipping flammable solvent-based paint (UN1263) and printing ink (UN1210) as dangerous goods. Most Chapter 32 goods are EAR99, so no **BIS** licence is needed for most destinations — but 26 Chapter 32 HS codes, including paints, TiO2 pigment, caulks and printing inks, need a licence for Russia and Belarus, and radar-absorbing or other signature-reduction coatings are controlled.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: The largest 2025 export lines were caulks and painters' fillings (3214.10, $932M), solvent-based paints on other polymers such as epoxies and polyurethanes (3208.90, $877M), titanium dioxide pigment with 80% or more TiO2 (3206.11, $873M) and acrylic or vinyl latex paint (3209.10, $760M). Titanium dioxide as a chemical (HS 2823) is Chapter 28; only pigments and preparations based on it are 3206.11 or 3206.19. Paint brushes and rollers (9603) and paintings (9701) are not Chapter 32.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Paints, coatings and inks often move through distributors; screen the end user named in the order, not only the distributor that pays.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Most Chapter 32 goods are EAR99. The exceptions are coatings and paints specially designed for reduced or tailored radar, infrared or ultraviolet signatures, controlled under ECCN 1C001 or 1C101 (or the U.S. Munitions List when specially designed for military use).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: 26 Chapter 32 HS codes are on BIS's Russia and Belarus industry-sector list (Supplement No. 4 to 15 CFR Part 746): tanning extracts and agents, natural colorants, 3204.90, color lakes, TiO2 pigment (3206.11), ultramarine and other pigments (3206.41, 3206.49), ceramic colors and frit, every paint and varnish code of 3208–3210, pigment dispersions (3212.90), caulks and fillers (3214) and printing inks (3215.11, 3215.19). Even EAR99 goods under those codes need a licence for Russia or Belarus.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Shipments to Canada, the largest buyer, are exempt from EEI unless they need a licence or are only passing through Canada to a third country (15 CFR 30.36).

rules.title: TSCA section 12(b): notify EPA through CDX of the export of a chemical substance or mixture subject to certain TSCA actions (section 4 or 5(b) data requirements, section 5 orders or rules, section 6 rules, section 7 actions), within seven days of forming the intent to export or on the export date, whichever is earlier; components under 1% (0.1% for carcinogens) are exempt

citations.label: EPA: TSCA requirements for exporting chemicals

rules.title: Flammable paints, varnishes, driers and solvent-based inks ship as Class 3 dangerous goods (UN1263 Paint or Paint related material; UN1210 Printing ink): classification, packaging, marking and documentation under the Hazardous Materials Regulations, which also underpin the ocean (IMDG) and air (IATA) rules; limited-quantity and combustible-liquid exceptions are in 49 CFR 173.150

Signature-reduction coatings: paints and coatings specially designed for reduced or tailored reflectivity or emissivity in the microwave, infrared or ultraviolet bands (ECCN 1C101 when usable in missiles and similar systems, 1C001 for electromagnetic-absorbing materials) need a licence for many destinations; items specially designed for military use fall under the ITAR instead

citations.label: Commerce Control List (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1), Category 1

rules.title: Russia and Belarus: a licence is required to export, reexport or transfer items under the HS codes listed in Supplement No. 4 to Part 746, EAR99 items included; 26 Chapter 32 codes are listed

groups.label: Natural colorants (plant & animal)
groups.note: Colorants sold in the U.S. for food, drugs or cosmetics fall under FDA's color additive rules (21 CFR Parts 70–82); these are U.S. market rules, not export permits.

groups.label: Synthetic organic dyes & pigments
groups.note: Only 3204.90 is on the Russia and Belarus list. FD&C synthetic colors and their lakes are batch-certified by FDA for U.S. use (21 CFR Part 80); that certification is not an export requirement.

groups.label: Titanium dioxide & other pigments
groups.note: Of this heading, TiO2 pigment (3206.11), ultramarine (3206.41) and other pigments (3206.49) are on the Russia and Belarus list; 3206.19, 3206.20, 3206.42 and 3206.50 are not.

groups.label: Solvent-based paints & varnishes
groups.note: Solvent-based paints and varnishes are usually flammable (UN1263) and ship as dangerous goods.

groups.label: Water-based paints & varnishes
groups.note: Water-based latex paints are usually not flammable; check the safety data sheet before shipping them as non-hazardous.

groups.label: Paint driers
groups.note: Driers are often supplied in flammable solvents.

groups.label: Pigment dispersions, stamping foils & retail dyes
groups.note: Pigments dispersed in non-aqueous media (3212.90) are on the Russia and Belarus list; stamping foils (3212.10) are not.

groups.label: Caulk, putty, mastics & fillers
groups.note: Most caulks and fillers are not dangerous goods, but solvent-based sealants can be flammable.

groups.label: Printing, writing & drawing inks
groups.note: Solvent-based printing inks ship as UN1210; black and color printing inks (3215.11, 3215.19) are on the Russia and Belarus list, writing and drawing inks (3215.90) are not.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Document U.S. origin to get the EU's 0% rate
savings.saves: The EU's normal duty of up to 6.5% on Chapter 32 goods (6% on TiO2 pigment, 6.5% on most paints, dyes and inks).
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin Chapter 32 goods imported into the EU from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2029 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1455, Annex I).
savings.document: Proof that the goods are of U.S. origin under the EU's non-preferential origin rules, such as a certificate of origin, until the EU and the U.S. agree preferential rules of origin.
savings.caveat: Goods made in a third country and only shipped from the U.S. do not qualify. The Commission can suspend the cut, and it ends December 31, 2029 unless extended.

savings.title: Have the Chinese buyer apply for a counter-tariff exclusion
savings.saves: China's 2019 counter-tariffs of 5%–25% and the 2.5% September 2019 layer on almost every Chapter 32 line (for example 22.5 points on U.S. solvent paint). The 10% extra duty on all U.S. goods still applies.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. Chapter 32 goods bought by a Chinese importer on commercial terms. Titanium dioxide pigments (3206.1110, 3206.1190) are on the eligible list; other lines can be added on request.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies through the exclusion system of the Tariff Commission (Ministry of Finance) and declares the exclusion number at customs.
savings.caveat: Exclusions under the November 2025 U.S.–China deal are valid until December 31, 2026; no extension has been announced. Duty already paid is not refunded.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
